title: Passover: cleaning without panic
hookLine: the rabbis say dust is not chametz; clean what matters
tomorrow: what if there's no child at the seder to ask?

lines: ELEVEN AT NIGHT, ON A STEPLADDER.
cards: It's eleven at night, a few days before Passover. Someone you love is up on a stepladder, wiping the blades of the ceiling fan with a wet rag, and the bathroom grout is next on the list. The dishwasher hums.
The playlist is on its third loop. Nobody has eaten a real dinner, because the kitchen is in pieces. Ask what the fan has to do with bread, and you'll get a look.
So here's the question that could end the standoff: does dust count?

teach.b: The Torah's rule is short. In the JPS 1917 translation: "Seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread; howbeit the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses."
Leaven, chametz in Hebrew, is grain dough that has risen: bread, cake, crackers, cereal. Then the rabbis ask the practical question.
The Mishnah, in its tractate on Passover, Pesachim, says you search for chametz by candlelight the night before, and that a place where chametz is never brought doesn't need searching.
The ceiling fan is off the list, unless someone eats up there. Now the part to tell a friend tonight.
After the search comes a short declaration in Aramaic: any chametz I didn't see and didn't find is canceled, and counts as the dust of the earth.
The tradition plans for the crumb you miss, and turns it into dust on purpose. So the line you may hear from rabbis before Passover, dust is not chametz, isn't a shortcut. It's the law's own shape.
Clean where food actually goes: the kitchen, the car seat with the cracker bag, the backpack.
Spring cleaning is fine if you love it.
It just isn't the mitzvah, and a family too worn out to sing at the seder has lost the point of the cleaning.

how: Before Passover, Jewish households that keep Passover clean the places where food is kept and eaten, search for chametz by candlelight the night before, and say a short declaration canceling any chametz they missed.

games.q: two hours before the search and you're wiped out. the garage needs sorting, and the backpack you eat lunch from hasn't been touched. where does the Mishnah point you?
o: the backpack: search where chametz is actually brought.
the garage: the bigger the job, the more it counts.
both, halfway, so nothing gets skipped entirely.
games.why: a place where chametz is never brought doesn't need searching. the backpack goes first; the garage can wait for a spring cleaning you actually enjoy.

practice: Look around the room you're in and pick one small place where food really goes: a counter, a desk drawer, a bag. Clear it slowly, one thing at a time, and breathe out each time you set something down.
When it's done, leave the rest of the room exactly as it is.

wordCard.voice: Passover: the spring festival of leaving Egypt, and before it, a search for chametz in the places food actually goes.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: dust is not chametz, and the crumb you miss already counts as dust. Day done.
